title: Automating Variational Quantum Sensing through Reinforcement-Learned Circuit Structures
abstract: Variational quantum sensing offers a promising route to high-precision parameter estimation, but its performance depends strongly on the circuit architectures used for probe preparation and measurement. Existing approaches typically optimize continuous parameters within predefined ansätze, restricting the accessible design space and limiting adaptation to sensing tasks and hardware constraints. Here, we introduce \textsc{AutoQSense}, a reinforcement-learning framework that searches circuit architectures using Fisher-information-based objectives. For few-qubit systems, a single agent sequentially constructs preparation and measurement circuits. For larger systems, a distributed formulation assigns local circuit design to subsystem agents and inter-block entanglement to a budgeted agent. Numerical results show that the learned architectures recover known benchmark strategies, adapt to dephasing noise, and outperform fixed hardware-efficient ansätze while using fewer entangling gates. These results establish \textsc{AutoQSense} as a resource-aware approach to adaptive and hardware-compatible quantum sensing.
summary: This paper introduces AutoQSense, an RL framework that automates the design of quantum sensing protocols by optimizing the circuit architecture itself, not just the parameters. By treating circuit design as a sequential decision process, it achieves superior sensitivity compared to fixed ansätze. This establishes a resource-aware methodology for adaptive quantum metrology applicable to large, complex quantum hardware.
main_problem: The core problem is automating Variational Quantum Sensing (VQS) by optimizing not only continuous variational parameters but also the underlying quantum circuit architectures themselves.
main_result: The proposed framework, AutoQSense, successfully learns adaptive, hardware-compatible quantum sensing protocols that outperform fixed, hardware-efficient ansätze while using fewer entangling gates.
method: It employs a nested optimization loop: an inner VQS loop optimizes parameters using quantum gradients, while an outer Reinforcement Learning (RL) loop updates the circuit architecture (the policy) based on the resulting Fisher Information.
model_or_system: The system is an $n$-qubit quantum processor used for parameter estimation. The methodology scales from single-agent search for small systems to a distributed multi-agent formulation for large, lattice-connected systems.
key_observables: Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) and Classical Fisher Information (CFI) are the primary objectives, used to define the RL reward function.
important_parameters: The optimization involves variational parameters ($	heta$) and the discrete architectural choices (gate sequences/connectivity $A, B$).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption addressed is that existing VQS methods are limited by fixed, a priori circuit ansätze, which the RL framework overcomes.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the AUTOQSENSE workflow, comparing its performance against benchmarks like the Standard Quantum Limit (SQL) and fixed ansätze, especially showing gains in QFI and reduced gate count.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the VQS problem, identifies the architectural limitation, proposes the RL framework (AutoQSense), details the single-agent and multi-agent implementations, and validates the approach by showing performance gains and structural insights.
why_interesting: The integration of RL for circuit design directly addresses the resource-aware optimization needed in quantum metrology, providing a systematic way to navigate the vast space of possible quantum circuits.

FIG. 2: Schematic of the multi-agent RL framework for distributed quantum-sensor architecture search. Each local agent observes its local state si and samples a local circuit action ki from its policy παi(ki|si). The local actions are assembled into a global circuit architecture k(1−M), which is evaluated by a centralized evaluator. The resulting CFI, together with the estimated local contribution, is used as the reward to update the local policies.
